title: Microsoft 365 Outage: Why Most of the Loss Will Stay Uninsured
summary: Loss modellers put insured losses from the November 12 Microsoft 365 disruption anywhere from under $100 million to about $1.4 billion. Our worked example shows why an 8 to 12 hour waiting period leaves a typical small business carrying 44% to 67% of its own outage loss.
description:
The Microsoft 365 disruption that began shortly after noon Eastern time on November 12 cut businesses off from Outlook, Exchange Online and Teams, with knock-on problems in SharePoint, OneDrive, Copilot and Defender XDR. Severe disruption lasted roughly 18 hours, and the full event, including degraded performance, ran for about 38 hours. It was Microsoft's second major Microsoft 365 failure of 2026, after a January outage of almost 10 hours.

Within days, cyber risk modellers published their first insured loss estimates. They do not agree. This PolicyRix Team analysis lines the estimates up, compares them with earlier cloud events, and works through what a typical cyber policy would actually pay a small business.

The estimates side by side

CyberCube said insured losses were most likely below $100 million, with an upper bound of about $350 million, and put the impact on global cyber premiums at 0% to 2% of loss ratio. Morningstar DBRS estimated $300 million to $500 million. Kovrr published a range of roughly $300 million to $1.4 billion, alongside an estimate of about $16 billion in lost productivity worldwide. Euler ILS gave a range of $100 million to $1 billion. Marsh Re did not give a figure but said it expected the market impact to be minimal.

On our arithmetic, the widest published range runs from $100 million to $1.4 billion, a fourteen-fold spread. Even within a single modeller, Euler's top estimate is ten times its bottom one. That spread is itself the main finding: nobody yet knows how many affected firms bought cover that responds to this kind of event.

How it compares

For the CrowdStrike software failure in July 2024, CyberCube estimated $400 million to $1.5 billion of insured losses. For the October 2025 Amazon Web Services outage, it estimated $38 million to $581 million. CyberCube's upper bound for the Microsoft event, $350 million, is about 88% of the bottom of its CrowdStrike range, and its central view of under $100 million is about a quarter of it. So on CyberCube's numbers this is a smaller insured event than CrowdStrike, despite running longer, mainly because many machines kept working locally and staff could switch to other tools.

The waiting-period problem

Most cyber policies that cover business interruption from an outside provider's system failure, often called dependent or contingent business interruption, include a waiting period. Typical waiting periods are 8 to 12 hours. Losses inside that window are not paid. Many policies also cover only malicious events at a provider, or exclude non-malicious system failures altogether, and this event was a technical failure, not an attack.

Take an illustrative business that loses $1,000 of profit for every hour its email and collaboration tools are down, and assume the policy does cover non-malicious failures at a provider.

With an 8-hour waiting period, an 18-hour severe outage costs $18,000. The policy responds to 10 hours, or $10,000, so the business carries $8,000, or about 44%.

With a 12-hour waiting period, the policy responds to 6 hours, or $6,000, and the business carries $12,000, or about 67%.

If the policy excludes non-malicious failures, the business carries 100%. Deductibles and sub-limits reduce recoveries further. These figures are our illustration, not a quote from any insurer.

Parametric cover is the other route. Some products pay a set amount when a monitored cloud service is down for a set time. It is not clear this event triggers them, because it hit a software service, Microsoft 365, rather than the underlying Azure cloud capacity many triggers track.

What a business owner should check

Open the cyber policy and look for three things: whether dependent business interruption is covered for system failure as well as security failure; the waiting period in hours; and any sub-limit for dependent business interruption. Then estimate the hourly cost of losing email and file access. If an 18-hour outage would hurt and the policy would pay little or nothing, a broker can quote a shorter waiting period or broader system-failure wording. Keeping an offline contact list and a backup way to reach customers costs far less than any premium.

What the data cannot tell us

The estimates are early and built from models, not claims. They do not say how many businesses had cover that responds to non-malicious provider failures, and that share drives the final number. Productivity loss is not the same as insured loss: Kovrr's $16 billion figure is a measure of disruption, not of claims. Outage length also differed by region and by service, so the 18-hour figure is a broad guide, not every firm's experience. Our worked example uses round numbers to show the mechanics.

The short version: the outage was long enough to test cyber policies, but the wording and waiting period, more than the headline loss estimates, decide whether a business gets paid.
source_name: PolicyRix Team analysis of loss estimates from CyberCube, Morningstar DBRS, Kovrr, Euler ILS and Marsh Re, with reporting from Insurance Business, Reinsurance News and Global Finance
image_alt: Data centre server racks with status lights (illustrative)
key_points: The November 12 Microsoft 365 disruption brought about 18 hours of severe outage and roughly 38 hours of total disruption.
Insured loss estimates range from under $100 million (CyberCube's central view) to about $1.4 billion (Kovrr's top end).
CyberCube's $350 million upper bound is about 88% of the bottom of its 2024 CrowdStrike range.
On our example, an 8 to 12 hour waiting period leaves a business carrying 44% to 67% of an 18-hour outage loss, even when cover applies.
Many cyber policies exclude non-malicious system failures at a provider, so check the wording, not just the limit.
why_it_matters: Almost every business relies on a handful of cloud providers. The gap between outage loss and insured loss shows owners where their own cover falls short before the next outage, not after it.

title: Asia Insurance Prices Fall Again, but Not for Japan or Motor Cover
summary: Aon says Asian commercial insurance prices fell 1% to 10% in the third quarter, with Indian property down more than 31%. Japan and motor cover in Japan and Korea moved the other way. We rank the markets and show what the ranges mean on a HK$1 million premium.
description:
Commercial insurance in Asia is still getting cheaper for most buyers, but the averages hide a split. Aon's Global Insurance Market Insights report for the third quarter of 2026 puts the overall Asia price change at a fall of 1% to 10%. Indian property fell by more than 31%. Japan bucked the trend with increases of 1% to 10%, and motor insurance in Japan and South Korea also rose.

This PolicyRix Team analysis ranks the country and line moves Aon reported, converts the ranges into money on an example premium, and checks them against Marsh's separate index.

The ranking

Using the midpoint of each Aon range, our ranking from biggest fall to biggest rise is:

India property: down more than 31%.
Hong Kong casualty: down 11% to 20%, a midpoint of about 15.5%.
China and Hong Kong directors and officers (D&O): down 11% to 20%, about 15.5%.
Asia overall: down 1% to 10%, about 5.5%.
Singapore casualty and Singapore motor: flat.
Japan overall, and Japan and Korea motor: up 1% to 10%, about 5.5%.

That is a gap of more than 36 percentage points between the cheapest-moving line and the dearest. Aon's Jon Pipe, head of commercial risk solutions for Asia, has described Japan as an outlier where insurers are refocusing on profit-based underwriting. Jamie Sparkes of Aon has pointed to strong competition and ample capacity across most other markets.

What the ranges mean in money

Take a Hong Kong company paying HK$1 million a year for casualty cover. A cut of 11% to 20% saves HK$110,000 to HK$200,000, or about HK$155,000 at the midpoint. A company in Singapore with the same casualty premium would, on Aon's figures, see little or no change. A Japanese firm with a ¥500,000 motor fleet premium would face an extra ¥5,000 to ¥50,000. These are illustrations based on Aon's ranges; individual renewals depend on claims records, exposure and the size of the account.

A second view

Marsh's Global Insurance Market Index for the same quarter showed Asia commercial rates down 6% on average, after a 5% fall in the second quarter, and Asia property down 7%. Marsh noted Vietnam as an exception, with property rates up 13% because of regulatory pricing tariffs. The two brokers measure differently, Aon in bands and Marsh as an average of its own client renewals, but both point in the same direction: falling prices for most commercial buyers, with pockets of increases tied to claims or regulation.

Why the split exists

Property prices are falling fastest because reinsurance is cheaper and insurers have spare capacity after strong profits. India's very large property cut reflects heavy competition among domestic insurers for corporate accounts. Motor is different everywhere: repair costs, parts prices and claims frequency keep rising, so insurers cannot cut. Japan's increases follow several years of poor underwriting results on corporate accounts and pressure on insurers to price for profit rather than market share.

What buyers should do

Buyers in falling markets have leverage at renewal. Brokers suggest using it for better terms as well as lower prices: higher limits, lower deductibles or broader wording, which last longer than a one-year discount. Buyers in Japan and in motor lines should start renewals early, show their risk controls and claims data, and test the market rather than accept the first increase. Everyone should remember that soft markets end; cutting limits to bank a saving can leave a gap when prices turn.

What the data cannot tell us

Aon reports ranges, not exact figures, so our midpoints are a simplification. A fall "of more than 31%" has no stated floor. The figures are averages across Aon's own client renewals and do not show how much of the change came from rate rather than changes in cover. They also say nothing about small businesses, which often buy packaged policies priced differently from large corporate programmes. And one quarter does not make a trend; prices for some lines can turn within a year.

The short version: most Asian buyers are paying less this year, and Hong Kong casualty buyers could save a sixth of their premium, but Japanese firms and motor buyers are still being asked for more.
source_name: PolicyRix Team analysis of Aon Global Insurance Market Insights Q3 2026 and Marsh Global Insurance Market Index Q3 2026
key_points: Aon says Asia commercial insurance prices fell 1% to 10% in Q3 2026; India property fell more than 31%.
Hong Kong casualty and China and Hong Kong D&O fell 11% to 20%, while Singapore casualty and motor were flat.
Japan overall and motor in Japan and Korea rose 1% to 10%.
On a HK$1 million casualty premium, Aon's range implies savings of HK$110,000 to HK$200,000.
Marsh's separate index shows Asia rates down 6% on average, with Vietnam property up 13% due to tariffs.
why_it_matters: Commercial insurance is a large fixed cost for Asian businesses. Knowing which markets and lines are softening helps buyers negotiate, and shows where prices are still rising.

title: When Insurers Leave, Home Values Fall: What Cotality's Data Shows
summary: Cotality links insurance nonrenewals to falling home values: in Dare County, North Carolina, 13% of policies were not renewed in 2023 and values fell about 10%. On a $400,000 home that is $40,000 of lost equity. We compare the US, Australian and storm-belt evidence.
description:
Home insurance is usually discussed as a monthly bill. New research from property data firm Cotality argues it is becoming a driver of home values too. In its report "Weather rewrites home value," Cotality sets out cases where insurers pulled back after disasters and local prices followed.

This PolicyRix Team analysis puts the main figures on a common scale, converts them into equity on a typical home, and sets out what they do and do not prove.

The cases, side by side

Dare County, North Carolina: in 2023, 13% of property insurance policies were not renewed, and home values fell by about 10%. By 2025, price growth had turned negative.

Lake County, California: nonrenewals reached 7.6% in 2023 after repeated wildfire seasons, and Cotality says rising insurance costs are pricing some residents out.

Winkler County, Texas: about a quarter of homeowners dropped their cover, according to the report.

Naples, Florida: price growth fell by 8.3%.

Expressed per 1,000 insured homes, that is 76 nonrenewals in Lake County, 130 in Dare County and about 250 households without cover in Winkler County. Those are large numbers for a single year. For comparison, nonrenewal rates in most US counties are in low single digits.

What it means in equity

A 10% fall on a $400,000 home in Dare County is $40,000 of lost equity, before any change in the insurance bill. For many families, home equity is their largest store of wealth, so a fall of this size matters more than a premium rise of a few hundred dollars a year. It also affects mortgage lending, since lenders require insurance and a falling value can push a borrower's loan-to-value ratio above key thresholds.

Australia offers a longer view

Cotality's Australian data looks at recovery after floods. In Lismore, New South Wales, home values remain about 5% below their pre-flood level. In southeast Queensland, which also flooded but recovered faster, values are about 31% above pre-flood levels. Applied to a home worth A$600,000 before the floods, the Lismore figure implies about A$570,000 today and the southeast Queensland figure about A$786,000, a gap of roughly A$216,000. That is our illustration of the gap, not a valuation of any home.

Storms are spreading the problem inland

The report says about 9.5 million homes in the US Midwest are in counties where severe-storm risk is rising. In Kiowa County, Colorado, Cotality projects an extra $1.4 million of storm losses by 2040. Allianz has estimated that severe convective storms, which bring hail, tornadoes and damaging winds, caused about $60 billion of insured losses worldwide in 2025. These storms do not get the headlines of hurricanes, but they now drive a large share of homeowner claims, which is why insurers in states far from the coast are raising prices and deductibles too.

Denise Moore and Anand Srinivasan of Cotality argue in the report that the answer is resilience: homes built or retrofitted to resist local hazards keep their insurability and therefore their value.

What homeowners and buyers can do

Buyers should get insurance quotes before making an offer, not after, and ask the seller for the current premium and claims history. Owners in areas where insurers are pulling back should look at mitigation that insurers reward: impact-rated roofs in hail and hurricane zones, cleared defensible space in wildfire areas, and raised utilities in flood zones. Many states offer grants for roof upgrades. Keeping proof of upgrades can also help when shopping for cover or selling.

What the data cannot tell us

The report shows that nonrenewals and price falls happened together; it does not prove that one caused the other. Storm damage, local jobs and wider housing market moves also affect values. The county figures come from different years and different hazards, so they are not a ranking. Our dollar figures apply one percentage to a single example home. And recovery is possible: southeast Queensland shows that values can rebound strongly where rebuilding and insurance return.

The short version: in places where insurers retreat, the cost to homeowners is showing up not only in premiums but in the value of the home itself.
source_name: PolicyRix Team analysis of Cotality's Weather Rewrites Home Value report (2026), with reporting from Claims Journal and Allianz severe convective storm estimates
key_points: In Dare County, North Carolina, 13% of policies were not renewed in 2023 and home values fell about 10%.
Lake County, California saw 7.6% nonrenewals in 2023; about a quarter of homeowners in Winkler County, Texas dropped cover.
A 10% fall on a $400,000 home is $40,000 of lost equity on our calculation.
In Australia, Lismore values are about 5% below pre-flood levels while southeast Queensland is about 31% above.
Cotality says 9.5 million Midwest homes are in counties with rising severe-storm risk.
why_it_matters: For most families, home equity is their biggest asset. If insurance retreat drags values down, the cost of climate risk lands on owners twice: in higher premiums and in a lower sale price.

title: MAIF Launches In-House Reinsurer With EUR 145m of Capital
summary: French mutual insurer MAIF has set up MAIF Reinsurance, a France-based subsidiary with EUR 145 million of equity that starts on January 1, 2027. It will pool risks from across the group as extreme weather and reinsurance prices put pressure on home and motor insurers.
description:
MAIF, one of France's largest mutual insurers, is creating its own reinsurance company. MAIF Reinsurance, based in France, has been approved by the French prudential supervisor, the Autorite de controle prudentiel et de resolution (ACPR), and will start operating on January 1, 2027 with EUR 145 million of equity.

What changed

The new subsidiary will take on part of the risks written by the group's insurers and pool them centrally, alongside the reinsurance MAIF already buys from outside reinsurers. It can serve every entity in the group, including SMACL Assurances, which insures local authorities, Altima, and life insurer MAIF VIE. Luc Delage, deputy chief executive of the MAIF group, will also be chief executive of MAIF Reinsurance.

MAIF says the move is a response to changing insurance risks, including more frequent extreme weather, and to swings in the price and availability of reinsurance. The group also noted that proposed changes to equalisation provisions in France's draft Finance Bill would make it easier for the subsidiary to operate, if lawmakers adopt them. Equalisation provisions let insurers set aside reserves in good years to absorb catastrophe losses in bad ones, with tax treatment that matters for how much they can hold.

The scale

MAIF serves more than 4 million members and reported revenue of nearly EUR 6 billion in 2025. On our arithmetic, the EUR 145 million of capital in the new reinsurer equals about 2.4% of that annual revenue. It is not designed to replace external reinsurance but to retain a slice of risk inside the group rather than paying a reinsurer to carry it.

Why insurers do this

Large insurers create in-house reinsurers, sometimes called captives, for three main reasons. Pooling risks from several companies in one place lets the group hold less capital overall, because losses in different businesses rarely peak at the same time. Retaining more risk means paying less margin to outside reinsurers when their prices are high. And a central vehicle gives the group a single buyer when it does go to the external market, which can win better terms.

The risk is that the group keeps more of its own catastrophe losses. In a year with severe storms, hail and floods, as France has seen several times recently, a larger retained share hits the group's results directly. The size of the capital base and the external protection bought above it decide how big that exposure is.

The French context

French home insurers have faced rising weather claims for several years. Hail, drought-related subsidence and flooding have pushed up losses, and the national natural catastrophe scheme, CatNat, has been put under strain. Insurers have responded with higher premiums, and some smaller mutuals have tightened what they write in the most exposed areas. Reinsurance prices rose sharply in 2023 before easing in 2025 and 2026, and MAIF's comments suggest it wants protection against the next spike.

What it means for MAIF members

For policyholders, nothing changes in their cover or claims process. The new company sits behind the insurers they deal with. Over time, if the structure lowers the group's reinsurance costs, it could help limit premium increases, though MAIF has made no promise on pricing. As a mutual, MAIF has no outside shareholders, so any savings stay inside the member-owned group. Members who want to understand their own exposure should check their home policy for natural catastrophe and storm sections, and how their excess applies to each.

What to watch

The key details still to come are how much risk the group will cede to the new reinsurer, how much external reinsurance it will buy on top, and whether the Finance Bill changes on equalisation provisions pass. Those will show whether MAIF Reinsurance is a modest pooling vehicle or a bigger shift in how the group manages catastrophe risk.
source_name: MAIF announcement via Coverager; ACPR register
key_points: MAIF has created MAIF Reinsurance, a France-based subsidiary with EUR 145 million of equity, approved by the ACPR.
It starts on January 1, 2027 and can serve all group entities, including SMACL Assurances, Altima and MAIF VIE.
Deputy group CEO Luc Delage will also lead the reinsurer.
The capital equals about 2.4% of MAIF's nearly EUR 6 billion 2025 revenue on our calculation.
MAIF cites extreme weather and reinsurance price swings; proposed Finance Bill changes on equalisation provisions would help.
why_it_matters: How insurers fund catastrophe risk shapes what members pay for home and motor cover. In-house reinsurance can cut costs but also means the group keeps more of its own storm losses.

title: Direct Line Home Cover Gets Higher Limits and Zero Emergency Excess
summary: Aviva has refreshed Direct Line's direct home insurance range across its Silver, Gold and Platinum tiers, with higher emergency and alternative accommodation limits, no excess for emergency access claims and a GBP 50 excess for frozen food. Existing customers move to the new wording at renewal.
description:
Aviva has updated the home insurance policies sold directly under the Direct Line brand, the first broad change to the range since Aviva bought Direct Line Group in 2025. The three tiers, Silver, Gold and Platinum, keep their names, but each now carries higher limits on several common claims and lower excesses on two.

What changed

According to Aviva, all three tiers now include:

No excess for emergency access claims, which cover damage caused when emergency services force entry to a home.
A reduced GBP 50 excess for frozen food claims, for food spoiled when a freezer fails or the power goes off.
Higher alternative accommodation limits for both buildings and contents cover, which pay for somewhere to stay if a home becomes uninhabitable after an insured event.
Enhanced cover for theft from outbuildings such as sheds and garages.
No administration fees for mid-term changes to a policy.

Aviva also said it has raised Home Emergency cover limits and increased cover for the belongings of family members studying away from home. New customers can buy the updated policies now; existing customers will move to them at their next renewal.

Dan Simson, head of Direct Line Home Insurance at Aviva, said home insurance should not stand still and that cover needs to evolve as customers' needs change.

What Aviva did not say

The announcement did not give the new limits in pounds, the previous frozen food excess, or how the three tiers differ. It also did not say whether premiums will change. Those details matter: a higher limit is only useful if it is high enough for a real claim, and the price of each tier decides whether the improvement is good value.

Why the changes matter in practice

Alternative accommodation is the limit most likely to be tested by a serious claim. After a flood or a fire, repairs can take many months, and rent for a family home can easily run to GBP 1,500 to GBP 2,500 a month in much of the UK, more in London. A limit that looked generous a few years ago may not last the length of a major repair today. Emergency access claims are smaller but common, and removing the excess means the full cost of a forced door or window is paid. A GBP 50 frozen food excess is low enough that a claim after a long power cut becomes worthwhile.

How this fits Aviva's strategy

Since buying Direct Line, Aviva has run the brand in two channels. In September it launched a separate Direct Line home range on price comparison websites for the first time, in Essentials, Standard and Premium tiers, starting with Confused.com. The refreshed Silver, Gold and Platinum policies are the direct range, sold through Direct Line's own website and phone lines. Keeping the two ranges distinct lets Aviva compete on price where shoppers compare quotes, while offering fuller cover to customers who come to the brand directly.

What policyholders should do

Existing Direct Line home customers should read their renewal documents when they arrive and compare the new limits with the old ones, especially for alternative accommodation and home emergency. Anyone shopping for cover should compare the policy wording, not only the price, across insurers: check the alternative accommodation limit, the standard excess, and whether accidental damage and home emergency are included or sold as extras. UK rules mean renewal prices for existing customers cannot be higher than the price offered to an equivalent new customer through the same channel, so it is still worth asking for a new-customer quote before renewing.

The bottom line: the refresh improves several everyday features of Direct Line home cover, but without published limits and prices, customers will need to read the documents to judge how much better it really is.
source_name: Aviva announcement via Insurance Edge and Coverager; Aviva newsroom (September 2026)
key_points: Aviva has refreshed Direct Line's direct home range across Silver, Gold and Platinum tiers.
All tiers now have no excess for emergency access claims and a GBP 50 excess for frozen food claims.
Alternative accommodation, home emergency, outbuilding theft and student belongings limits have been raised.
New customers can buy now; existing customers move to the new policies at renewal.
Aviva did not publish the new limits or prices, so customers should compare their renewal documents.
why_it_matters: Direct Line is one of the UK's biggest home insurance brands. Higher limits and lower excesses change what customers get back after common claims, and set a benchmark rivals may follow.

title: Ghost Brokers: One New Fake Car Insurance Network Found Every Day
summary: The Insurance Fraud Bureau received reports of 596 suspected ghost broking networks in a year, about 1.6 a day, and AI is making fake policies harder to spot. Here is how the scam works, what it costs honest drivers, and the checks that take two minutes.
description:
Ghost broking, where fraudsters sell fake or invalid car insurance, is growing in the UK, and this week's Fraud Awareness Week has put it back in focus. The Insurance Fraud Bureau (IFB) says it received reports of 596 suspected organised ghost broking networks in the 12 months to September 2026. On our arithmetic, that is about 1.6 new networks a day. The IFB says each can target thousands of people through social media and messaging groups.

How the scam works

A ghost broker advertises cheap car insurance, usually on social media, in messaging groups or in community forums. The price is well below what a genuine insurer would charge, often aimed at young drivers or people who have struggled to find affordable cover. The fraudster either takes out a real policy using false details, such as a different address or no claims history, which the insurer then cancels, or sells a policy that never existed.

The newer version is harder to spot. Writing for Fraud Awareness Week, Manjit Rana of Clearspeed noted that some scams now bypass insurers entirely. No application reaches an insurer, so insurers' fraud checks never see it. AI tools let criminals produce convincing websites, emails and policy documents in minutes, so looking legitimate is no longer a sign of being legitimate.

The numbers

The IFB recorded a 52% rise in ghost broking cases between 2022 and 2024. Action Fraud logged 870 reports of insurance broker fraud in the year to September 2025, up 12% on the year before. Synectics Solutions found the number of ghost broking victims rose 93% in 2025. Research cited by Clearspeed found 39% of young drivers lack confidence in spotting a fake policy. Aviva has reported an eightfold rise in its takedowns of ghost broking adverts.

Victims pay twice. They lose the money they paid, and they are driving uninsured, which in the UK can mean a fixed penalty of GBP 300 and six penalty points, an unlimited fine if the case goes to court, and possible seizure of the car. If they crash, they can be personally liable for the other party's costs.

What it costs everyone else

Motor insurance fraud of all kinds is estimated to add GBP 50 to GBP 60 to every UK car policy. Across around 33 million insured vehicles, our calculation puts that at about GBP 1.65 billion to GBP 1.98 billion a year paid by honest drivers. Ghost broking is only part of that total, but it is one of the fastest-growing parts.

The two-minute checks

Check the seller on the Financial Conduct Authority register, which lists every firm allowed to arrange insurance. Search the register yourself; do not use a link or number the seller gives you.

Call the insurer named on the documents, using a phone number from the insurer's own website, and ask them to confirm the policy is live.

Check the Motor Insurance Database at askMID, which shows whether a vehicle is insured. A real policy normally appears within days.

Be wary of payment by bank transfer to a personal account, pressure to buy quickly, or a price far below other quotes.

For drivers struggling with cost, genuine options include telematics (black box) policies, adding an experienced named driver honestly, choosing a higher voluntary excess, or using a specialist broker for young or high-risk drivers.

What is being done

The IFB has launched a multilingual campaign, Ghost Broking: See Through the Scam, with the Association of British Insurers, the Chartered Insurance Institute, the City of London Police's Insurance Fraud Enforcement Department and the FCA. Industry voices are also calling on social media platforms to verify who is behind insurance adverts and stop banned operators reappearing under new accounts.

Anyone who thinks they have bought a fake policy should stop driving the car, contact the named insurer, and report it to Action Fraud and the IFB.
source_name: Insurance Fraud Bureau, Action Fraud, Insurance Edge (Clearspeed, Fraud Awareness Week), Insurance Times, Insurance Business and Insurance Age
key_points: The IFB received reports of 596 suspected ghost broking networks in the year to September 2026, about 1.6 a day.
Some scams now bypass insurers entirely, and AI makes fake documents look genuine.
Ghost broking cases rose 52% from 2022 to 2024; victims rose 93% in 2025 according to Synectics.
Motor fraud adds GBP 50 to GBP 60 per policy, about GBP 1.65 billion to GBP 1.98 billion a year across 33 million vehicles on our calculation.
Check the FCA register and askMID, and call the insurer directly before paying.
why_it_matters: Victims lose their money and end up driving uninsured, facing fines, points and personal liability. Fraud also pushes up premiums for every honest driver.
